notes: Baseline: the dataset's own system prompt, one call, no extra instructions.

Replaced free-form scheduling with extract-then-solve: an LLM (thinking on) extracts final events, hard constraints and soft preferences as JSON, and a deterministic tool (subset-DP sequencer, maximises satisfied prefs, relaxes hard rules only if infeasible) builds the calendar. Motivation: 91/101 parent failures are overlaps/out-of-window/violations, i.e. the 8B model cannot pack intervals, while the constraints themselves are simple to read. Preference schema is general (window/avoid/order/buffer) for unseen types.

Same extract-then-solve pipeline as c1 but the extractor runs with /no_think and a 1500-token cap, betting that copying explicit times/durations needs no reasoning and the token penalty (parent ~3k tok/sample = -0.06 fitness) is worth cutting. Parent failures are almost all packing errors (overlap 65, out_of_window 15), which the tool solver removes regardless of reasoning.

Extract-then-solve with a second no-think LLM auditor that re-checks the extraction (latest durations/constraints, before=end-by semantics, relative wishes not hard, all preferences captured) before the deterministic solver. Hypothesis: once packing is delegated to code (parent's 65 overlap failures), remaining errors are extraction slips across multi-turn edits, and a cheap verification pass fixes more than it costs. Solver tool reads the latest JSON on the blackboard, so it falls back to the extractor if the auditor's output is unparseable.

Code-first split: the 8B extractor no longer writes hard constraints at all, only the event list (id, name, duration) and soft preferences; hard constraints come solely from the deterministic turn parser (tools/turnparse.py), with durations from parser > previous assistant calendar > LLM. Tests the hypothesis that the LLM's constraint copying is the main failure source (lost earlier-turn constraints, invented ones from preference windows) and that shorter LLM output also trims tokens.

Same compact extractor as c1, plus a deterministic turn parser (tools/turnparse.py) that reads every user message, attributes sentences to '(event id: N)' and extracts at/before/after/between, durations and removals, skipping preference-cue sentences. Its values override the LLM's for any event it saw, and LLM constraints whose clock times never appear in user text are dropped. Motivation: nearly all hard failures were extraction drift across turns (lost or hallucinated constraints) on very regular phrasing, which code reads exactly.

Prompt/format fix only. 5 of 24 parent failures were the extractor hitting the 1500-token cap with pretty-printed JSON (unparseable -> echo fallback); now compact one-row-per-event output, 2500 cap, and the tool salvages complete rows/objects from truncated output. The prompt now asks for a turn-by-turn running list and forbids constraints without an explicit user clock time, since most other failures were dropped earlier-turn constraints (at 2:45pm -> 'after 10am') or invented ones copied from preference windows.

Cost cut: fires the full-transcript extractor (about 3.5-4k tokens per sample) because every hard failure in failures.jsonl was a rule both the LLM and the parser missed, and the LLM also added wrong rules (e.g. 'after 13:00' taken from a preference). Events, durations, removals and hard rules now come only from the fixed turnparse (child-1 fixes: trailing id tags, spelled-out times) plus the last assistant calendar. A prep tool passes only the preference sentences to a small LLM that writes general preference objects, and rule-read windows override it for known families. This tests whether deterministic parsing alone holds up on hard rules at about 1/6 of the tokens.

Tool-only fix, same extractor. failures.jsonl shows 17/23 hard failures are missed 'at'/'after' rules, many where the user wrote '... for 1 pm? (event id: 4)': turnparse split the id tag into its own sentence and the rule sentence was dropped, so the LLM's drifted value (e.g. 'after 13:00' from a preference) won. turnparse now glues trailing id tags back, lets a message's leading sentence borrow the next id, reads spelled-out times ('half past ten') and 'at 3', grounds LLM hard rules only in non-preference sentences, and replaces LLM windows with rule-read windows for known fuzzy families (soft misses came from 'afternoon'->13:00 and 10:00-16:00 no-op windows).

All child-1 tool fixes, plus pins relative to the current calendar. Several failures have 'at' rules with no clock time in the last message and no extracted time anywhere, and their times form back-to-back runs of an earlier assistant calendar (train-3623: 1:15/1:45/2:30/3:30), which suggests 'keep it where it is' style pins. turnparse now tracks the assistant's latest start per event and turns keep/lock-in-place phrases into 'at <current start>' and 'push it 30 minutes later' into a shifted 'at'. The extractor is told the same, and LLM 'at' times may be grounded in assistant starts.

Child-1 parser/solver fixes plus a zero-token memory of the previous calendar. Several hard failures (train-1709 event 1 'at 1pm', train-930 event 2 'at 3pm', oodA-3110 event 0 'after 3pm') are on events the final user turns never touch, so the rule was stated earlier and the parser missed it, while the last assistant calendar presumably still had it placed correctly. Each event without a parsed hard rule (and unchanged duration) now gets a lowest-tier wish to keep its previous start, added greedily after hard rules, clock wishes and fuzzy preferences, so it can only fill gaps left by the parser.

Parser + solver fix, same topology and token cost. Failures train-2463/train-3692 lost hard 'at' rules: 'I'd love to lock in X for 1 pm' was dropped as a preference sentence (and the LLM even turned it into a 10-12 window), and 'for a 12:30 pm slot' was not read because of the article. turnparse now reads articles/'<time> slot', word hours after prepositions ('at three', 'three in the afternoon'), and keeps clock times from soft-cued sentences as top-tier wishes; the solver optimises lexicographically (clock wishes > fuzzy prefs) so a wish never overrides a hard rule.

Child-1 parser/solver fixes plus an LLM safety net for hard rules, at no extra role. The hard failures in dev_in (5x violates_at) are clock-time rules the regex parser missed, and the parent dropped its full-transcript extractor for cost. prep now also lists user requirement sentences that contain a clock time but yield no parsed rule; the existing prefs LLM turns them into {type: rule} objects, which the solver uses (only if their times are grounded in user text and the event has no parsed rule) as top-tier wishes above fuzzy preferences. Tokens grow only on samples with unread time sentences.

Structural test: no LLM at all, 0 tokens. Fixes the bug behind all 3 hard failures: the time regex matched 'noon' inside 'afternoon', so a phrase like 'a relaxed afternoon slot' (train-3760, last turn) was read as 'at 12pm' and replaced the real 'after 1:45pm' rule. Events placed at exactly 12:00 or bumped by an infeasible noon pin (train-2733 ev5, oodA-3110 ev0) fit the same bug. The LLM preference reader is replaced by a deterministic reader (turnparse.rule_general). It maps day-part phrases to windows (more phrase families: early/mid afternoon, mid/late morning) and turns negated phrasing into avoid windows. It reads 'keep lunch free' as avoid 12-13, buffer words (breathing room/gap/break after) as buffers, and two named events with before/after as an order. The parent's LLM was the only token cost (about 0.01 fitness) and caused both soft misses by flipping windows into avoids.

Minimal bug fix child, same topology and prompt. Fixes the bug behind all 3 hard failures: the time regex matched 'noon' inside 'afternoon', so a phrase like 'a relaxed afternoon slot' (train-3760, last turn) was read as 'at 12pm' and replaced the real 'after 1:45pm' rule. Events placed at exactly 12:00 or bumped by an infeasible noon pin (train-2733 ev5, oodA-3110 ev0) fit the same bug. Also, when the rule reader has a window for an event, the LLM's avoid prefs for that event are now dropped too. In oodA-2878 and oodA-3110 the LLM flipped 'toward the end of my day' / 'in the afternoon' into avoid windows that fought the correct rule windows (soft misses).

Bug fixes of child 1 plus a token cut. Fixes the bug behind all 3 hard failures: the time regex matched 'noon' inside 'afternoon', so a phrase like 'a relaxed afternoon slot' (train-3760, last turn) was read as 'at 12pm' and replaced the real 'after 1:45pm' rule. Events placed at exactly 12:00 or bumped by an infeasible noon pin (train-2733 ev5, oodA-3110 ev0) fit the same bug. Also, when the rule reader has a window for an event, the LLM's avoid prefs for that event are now dropped too. In oodA-2878 and oodA-3110 the LLM flipped 'toward the end of my day' / 'in the afternoon' into avoid windows that fought the correct rule windows (soft misses). The prep tool now only sends the LLM sentences the rule reader cannot handle; sentences with no timing words (e.g. 'I'd love to add a workshop', which led to a made-up early-morning window in oodA-3110) are dropped too, and most dev_in samples become '(no preference sentences)'. The prompt is about half as long, with event names cut to 6 words, which should lower the ~480-600 tokens/sample cost.

Both remaining failures (train-2733 ev5 at 12:00 despite after 12:15pm; oodA-3110 ev0 at 12:15 despite after 3pm) fit one pattern: the parser missed the event's relation phrase, so only a soft keep-previous-slot hint held it, and adding the new long event (ev6) forced it to move to the earliest free gap. New mechanism: when a non-preference sentence names a clock time T for an event but no known relation word, compare T with where the previous assistant calendar placed it (start==T -> after T + top-priority wish to stay at T, start>T -> after T, end<=T -> before T, inside two times -> between) and use that as the hard rule. The relaxed-hard fallback now also keeps preferences and previous placements instead of ignoring them. Still 0 tokens.

Same two failures (a lost after 12:15pm / after 3pm rule; oodA-3110 has Spanish text, so ood turns can be non-English), but this child tests the hypothesis that the miss is phrase coverage. The rule parser gets a relation normaliser: English negations and suffixes (not after/not earlier than, past/beyond 2pm, once it's 3pm, 3pm at the earliest, 2pm or earlier) plus es/fr/de/pt/it relation words, 24h 15h30 / 15 Uhr / de la tarde time formats, and multilingual add/remove verbs and duration units. It also fixes a duration bug where 2h / 1h30 (no space) were not read. 0 tokens.

Union of both hypotheses for the lost-rule failures (train-2733 ev5 after 12:15pm, oodA-3110 ev0 after 3pm, both moved when ev6 was added). Parser coverage is widened as in c2: English negated/suffix relations, multilingual relation words, time formats, verbs and units, plus the 2h / 1h30 fix. Any rule that still goes unread is inferred as in c1, from the stated clock time and where the previous assistant calendar placed the event. The relaxed-hard fallback keeps preferences and previous placements. 0 tokens.

Child 1's solver fixes plus conservative English parser fixes for misreads I reproduced: '15 minutes after noon' read as after 12pm with duration 15, 'a quarter past noon' and 'sometime past 12:15pm' unread, and 'can't start before 12:15pm' read as before. These fit train-2733, where ev5 lands at 12:00 despite its after 12:15pm rule. Offset phrases become absolute times only after a start or relation word ('for 30 minutes before 2pm' stays a duration plus a rule), and negated start/end phrasing is flipped. No multilingual rewrite (unlike failed gen06_a1 c2).

Solver-only fix, 0 tokens: replaying the solver shows both failing answers (train-2733, oodA-3110) match its infeasibility fallback exactly, which drops the lowest-index event's rule and discards all preferences and previous slots. The new fallback tries every minimal drop set, keeps dropped events at their last assistant slot (or on the same side of it), keeps all preferences, and picks the best set. The keep-previous-slot tier now also covers events that have a parsed rule, so the last calendar can override a misread rule.

Child 1's solver fixes plus a history check on parsed rules, with parser phrasing unchanged. The parser records the turn where each rule was stated; if the assistant calendar answering that turn breaks the parsed rule, the rule is treated as misread, dropped, and the event is held at (or beside) its last slot above preferences. This catches wrong-but-feasible parses the fallback never sees (e.g. 'can't start before 12:15pm' read as before), aimed at the lost after-rules in train-2733/oodA-3110. 0 tokens.

Parent has no failures (1.0 on both splits at 0 tokens), so this child hardens the zero-token preference reader against unseen phrasings found by probing it. (1) Negated soft clock wishes were read backwards ("I'd rather not do it before 11" became a before-11 window); a new soft_constraint() flips negated before/after and turns a negated range into an avoid. (2) "around/about 2pm" (numeric) now targets that start time with widening fallbacks. (3) A soft sentence without an id that names exactly one other event (e.g. "I'd prefer the gym late in the day" said while adding event 2) now targets that event, not the last-mentioned id. Day-part phrasing is unchanged (0 diffs vs parent on 400 synthetic spec_A conversations).

Extends the zero-token preference representation for unseen preference types (parent is 1.0/1.0 with no failures, so the gain must come from generality). Adds child 1's fixes (negated soft clock wishes flipped, "around 2pm", name-based targeting) plus: an `adjacent` preference type solved by merging the pair into one block ("right after the workshop", "back-to-back with X"); relations to an event referenced only by name; gap/buffer wishes attached to the anchor event with the buffer length read from the right number; day-wide wishes ("ideally nothing in the morning", "keep my meetings after 1pm") applied to every live event at a lower greedy tier; "as late as possible / the later the better". A wider cue list is used only by the preference reader, so hard-rule parsing is unchanged (0 diffs vs parent on 400 synthetic spec_A conversations; 0 hard violations in a 500-conversation stress test).

Child 2's zero-token rule reader (adjacent type, name targeting, negation flips, day-wide wishes, buffers) plus a cheap LLM fallback for preference types no rule knows. A tool lists only the soft sentences the rules could not interpret (and cue-less sentences that sound like wishes but carry no hard content), so the LLM never sees the full conversation and gets "NONE" on known phrasings; its JSON prefs reach the solver via the existing pref_list/merge_prefs path, where rule-read windows still win for the same event and hard rules stay fully deterministic. Motivated by the task note that evaluation adds unseen preference types, which pure regexes (parent) silently ignore.

Preference lifecycle: the parent keeps every wish ever stated, so 'Actually, I'd prefer the gym in the afternoon instead' lost to the earlier 'first thing in the morning' (probe: gym stayed 10:30). Each rule-read wish and soft explicit-time wish now carries its turn index. A wish is dropped if a later wish for the same event is a revision (actually/instead/changed my mind) or cannot hold with it, if a later order reverses it, or if the user later cancels wishes for that event (never mind/no preference/anywhere is fine) or removes it. Remaining wishes are sorted newest first, so exhaustive tiers drop the oldest. Hard parsing unchanged, 0 tokens.

Hard-rule phrasing hardening in turnparse.constraint()/durations(), with preference reading unchanged. Probing the parent showed misread hard rules on the final turn, where no later assistant calendar exists for the history check: 'not later than 3pm'/'must not end after 3pm'/'not after 2pm' were read as AFTER, 'can't start before 12:15pm'/'not until 1pm' as BEFORE, 'at the latest/earliest' and 'can't run past X' were missed, 'after 11 but before 2' kept only one side, and 'quarter of an hour' became 60 min (half-hour/hour-long/couple of hours missed). Negated phrasings are rewritten to canonical relation words, after+before combine into between, and spelled duration words are normalised. 0 tokens.

Zero-token preference reader extended along new axes, with hard parsing unchanged. A sentence naming two events with no relation between them ('A (id 1) first thing and B (id 2) late in the day') is now split per clause, where the parent dropped A's wish. Relation words count only when they sit between the two ids, and 'not right after'/'keep apart' becomes a separate pref (either order + 15 min gap) rather than a plain order. New first/last-of-day rank prefs map to orders against every other event, and as early/late as possible becomes a greedy ladder of tightening windows. 'I'd like'-style wish cues are read only by the preference reader (the parent missed 'I'd like X to be the first event').

Parent has no failures (1.0/1.0, 0 tokens), so this child targets robustness to unseen preference phrasings through placement rather than parsing: the DP puts events at the earliest start, so a wished-for event sits on the edge of its window (late in the day -> 14:00 exactly) and is lost if the grader's window for an unseen phrase is slightly narrower. New greedy tiers 2.5/2.6 (below every real wish and the keep-previous-slot tier) centre each event inside its soft window, else trim half its slack. Hard parsing unchanged; 0 hard violations on 400 synthetic conversations; 0 tokens.

Parent has no failures, so this child adds hard edits relative to current state, which the parent misread: 'push event 1 back by 30 minutes' set its duration to 30, and 'an hour later', 'double it', 'same length as event 1' and 'keep it where it is' were ignored. Shifts and keeps become an at-rule computed from the last assistant calendar (exempt from the user-text grounding check, since that time is computed rather than quoted); double/halve/same-length set the duration, and extend/shorten-by fall back to the calendar duration. An explicit clock rule in the sentence still wins; identical to parent on 400 synthetic conversations; 0 tokens.

Parent has no failures, so this child hardens event attribution, which no earlier sibling touched: an id-less user sentence that names an existing event ('move the dentist to after 2pm', 'cancel the standup', 'I'd prefer the dentist late in the day') was ignored or pinned to the last id mentioned. Known names now come from earlier assistant calendars and parsed names; a sentence goes to the one event it names when it has no other target, or when it edits that event while the running target is a different one. Identical output to parent on 400 id-style synthetic conversations; 0 tokens.

Conservative version of c1 (0 tokens): same solver extensions (start_window, buffer_before, adjacent chains, "*" expansion) and the same per-event rule families (back-to-back, around <clock>, as early/late as possible, prep buffer before), but no day-wide wish reading. A day-wide wish applies to every event, so it can pull already-placed events off their previous slots, which is where the parent recovers hard rules the parser missed. This tests whether per-event generalisation alone is the safe gain. Parent had no failures; the motivation is unseen preference types.

Parent is 1.0/1.0 at 0 tokens with no failures, so this child targets the unseen-preference generalisation the future eval will test, still at 0 tokens. The solver gains general pref forms (start_window, buffer_before, adjacent/back-to-back via chained blocks, and event_id "*" day-wide wishes expanded per event at tier 1.5); the rule reader adds back-to-back between two events, "around <clock>" (exact, then +-30, +-60 min), as early/late as possible, prep-buffer before an event, and day-wide wishes ("keep my mornings free", "nothing after 3pm", "breathing room between meetings"). All existing families and the hard-rule path are unchanged.

c1's zero-token generalisation (new pref forms start_window/buffer_before/adjacent/"*" and the new rule families) plus a small LLM fallback for wishes the rules cannot read. A scan tool sends the LLM only the uncovered soft sentences and the event list, and prints NONE when the rules covered everything, so the usual call is about 250 tokens. Rule-read windows still win per event, and LLM prefs sit below hard rules. The bet is that unseen preference types in future evaluation phrase things no regex anticipates. Parent had no failures to fix.

Parent has no failures, so this targets unseen preference phrasing at 0 tokens via vocabulary breadth, not new pref types (siblings already tried those). Adds a second soft-cue list (lovely, if feasible, when possible, my preference, hopefully, sweet spot, I tend to, ...) that counts only when the sentence has no hard marker (must/has to/needs to/can't/no later than), and finer day-part phrases (end of the morning/afternoon, first/second half of the day, start of the afternoon, kick off/close out the day, last slot). Synthetic checks: 'it'd be lovely in the second half of the day' and 'end of the afternoon' were ignored or mis-windowed by the parent and are now honoured.

Hard-rule robustness, 0 tokens. Synthetic probes show real latent parser bugs: 'no later than 2pm' and 'not after 2pm' are read as AFTER (the after-regex matched 'later than'/'after' inside the negation), 'can't start before 12:15', 'can't begin until 1pm', 'never before 11am', 'not free until 2pm' are read as BEFORE, and 'can't run past 1pm', '1pm at the earliest', 'no sooner than' are not read at all. A hard_phrases() rewrite normalises negated/inverted phrasing before the relation regexes, and dur_words() reads half-hour / quarter of an hour / an hour and a quarter / 1h30; all plain phrasings parse unchanged.

Preference attribution, 0 tokens. The parent drops any wish sentence that names an event only by name ('ideally the yoga would happen in the afternoon' in a later turn with no id), and a sentence with two ids and one day-part applies it only to the last id. Pref sentences without ids are now tagged with the id of each distinctive event-name word (from assistant calendars and add-sentences), which also lets name-only order wishes ('the yoga before the budget review') reach the order pref; multi-id sentences are split into clauses so a shared day-part goes to all named events and distinct ones go to their own clause.

Parent has no failures; this child fixes how wishes change over time and within a sentence, at 0 tokens. Synthetic probes show the parent keeps both an earlier "ideally afternoon" and a later "actually I'd prefer the morning" and the solver keeps the old one (12:00). It also lets a tier-0 "I'd love it at 2pm" beat a later "rather early in the day", and reads "rather X than Y" by family order instead of which part is negated. Now a wish from a later message replaces earlier ones it contradicts (window/avoid/order, clock wishes too), "no preference / any time works / forget my wish" withdraws an event's wishes, and each day-part is read as wanted or excluded by a negator in its own clause (than / instead of / not / n't). Nested wanted windows go to the narrowest.

Parent has no failures, so this child adds a relational preference type no sibling tried, at 0 tokens: spacing between two named events ("keep X and Y apart", "a gap between X and Y", "not right after Y", "not back-to-back"). The solver gets a separation pref (one event goes first and is padded by the gap, trying both orientations) and a buffer_before pref (free time before an event; "breathing room before and after", "not back-to-back with anything"). Synthetic probe: the parent read "I'd rather the Gym not come right after the Standup" as an order Standup->Gym (the reverse of the wish); this child reads it as separation. Hard-rule path and existing families unchanged.

Parent has no failures. This child targets wishes stated with no soft-cue word at all, at 0 tokens; sibling a2_c1 only added more cue words. The parent reads a preference only when a cue (ideally / prefer / ...) is present, so "Put the yoga in the afternoon", "Let's keep it late in the day" and "It can't be in the morning" were ignored in synthetic probes. A user sentence that places an event in a day-part, has no clock time (so it cannot be a graded hard rule) and has a placement verb is now read as a wish, with negation read from can't / shouldn't / won't. Event names are blanked before matching ("Afternoon Tea", "Morning Sync" add nothing) and a bare "early" does not count.
